headline: Hungary opens its old secret police files

sources.title: Secret police files released in Hungary, 37 years after fall of communism (BBC News)
Hungary opens communist-era informer files in belated reckoning with Cold War past (Reuters, via Internazionale)
Hungary opens communist-era secret police files: But does a name in the database mean someone was an informer? (Daily News Hungary)
Hungary to open Communist-era informer files in reckoning with Cold War past (Reuters, via The Star)

chunks.text: On November 4, 2026, Hungary, a country in central Europe, put about 60,000 names on a website. They belong to people recruited, or asked to help, by its old [[secret police]]. The secret police were officers who watched citizens during 45 years of [[communist rule]]. Now anyone can {{look up}} a name. Some families may {{find out}} a [[deceased]] relative was an [[informer]], a person who secretly reports on others. On that date in 1956, Soviet tanks entered Budapest, the capital, to {{put down}} a [[pro-democracy]] [[uprising]].

verbs.correct: To find a name or fact in a record
verbs.wrong: To print a copy of a record
verbs.why: I look up new words in my dictionary. Students look up dates in the school library. Now anyone can look up a name on the website.

verbs.correct: To learn something you did not know
verbs.wrong: To make a secret file public
verbs.why: Many people find out the truth years later. Parents often find out about a problem from the school. Some Hungarian families may find out that a deceased relative was an informer.

verbs.correct: To stop an uprising with force
verbs.wrong: To start talks with a rebel group
verbs.why: Some rulers put down protests with soldiers. Strong armies put down rebellions quickly. In 1956, Soviet tanks entered Budapest to put down a pro-democracy uprising.

chunks.text: The secret police needed help from [[ordinary people]]. Informers watched friends, neighbors and [[coworkers]] and {{passed on}} what they learned. Many were [[blackmailed]], with [[threats]] like losing a job. An [[estimated]] 150,000 to 160,000 people were recruited as informers between 1944 and 1990. But the records are [[far from complete]]. Many files were [[shredded]] as communist rule {{fell apart}}.

verbs.why: Good nurses pass on the doctor's message to the family. Reporters pass on news from people they trust. Informers watched people around them and passed on what they learned.

verbs.wrong: To lose an election by a little
verbs.why: A small business falls apart when the money stops. Some governments fall apart during hard times. Many files were shredded as communist rule fell apart in Hungary.

chunks.text: Communist rule ended in 1989, but left and right governments {{put off}} opening the files. Since 1998, people have been able to ask for their own file. But many names were {{blacked out}}, and the new spy agencies {{held back}} many files. Hungary's prime minister, who won a [[landslide victory]] in April 2026, made opening the files a [[campaign promise]].

verbs.why: Many people put off going to the doctor. Cities often put off costly repairs. For decades, both left and right Hungarian governments put off opening the files.

verbs.correct: To cover words with dark ink
verbs.wrong: To copy words in a new file
verbs.why: Officials often black out names in old records. Lawyers black out private details in court papers. In the files people could request, many names were blacked out.

verbs.wrong: To send something to a court
verbs.why: Police sometimes hold back details of a crime. Some companies hold back their sales numbers. After 1989, the new spy agencies held back many secret police files.

chunks.text: [[Historians]] warn that a name on the website does not prove someone was an informer. Some people {{turned down}} requests to become informers and still {{ended up}} in the records. The website {{leaves out}} the reports informers wrote, to protect those they watched. Longer files on how people were recruited will {{come out}} by February 25, 2027. [[Critics]] say the website comes too late and may cause [[division]] and pain. The government says the website will help Hungarians {{get over}} those painful years. The prime minister asked people to treat the files with [[dignity]].

verbs.correct: To say no to a request or offer
verbs.why: She turns down the job because the pay is low. Many students turn down offers from expensive colleges. Some Hungarians turned down requests to become informers and still ended up in the records.

verbs.correct: To finally be in a certain place
verbs.wrong: To request a copy of a record
verbs.why: Lost letters often end up in the wrong office. Many old photos end up in a box in the attic. Some people who refused to help the secret police still ended up in the records.

verbs.wrong: To check if something is true
verbs.why: Some news reports leave out important facts. The short version of the book leaves out a few chapters. The website leaves out the reports informers wrote, to protect the people they watched.

verbs.wrong: To be read by the police
verbs.why: New job numbers come out every month. Test results come out in June. Longer files on how people were recruited will come out by February 25, 2027.

verbs.correct: To feel better after something painful
verbs.wrong: To write a book about a hard time
verbs.why: Most people get over a bad breakup with time. Children often get over a scary event quickly. The Hungarian government says the website will help people get over those painful years.

wordDefs.def: Police who secretly watch people for the government
ex: People were afraid to talk because of the secret police.
The secret police kept a file on the famous writer.
Many countries had a secret police force during the Cold War.

wordDefs.def: A time when one communist party controls a country
ex: My grandparents lived under communist rule.
Travel abroad was hard under communist rule.
The museum shows daily life during communist rule.
The money goes to the children of the deceased owner.
She keeps photos of her deceased husband.
The form asks for the name of the deceased person.

wordDefs.def: A person who secretly gives others information about someone
ex: The police paid an informer for the tip.
He learned that his best friend was an informer.
An informer told the police about the plan.

wordDefs.def: Supporting a system where people vote for their leaders
ex: Thousands joined the pro-democracy march.
She leads a pro-democracy group at her college.
A pro-democracy leader spoke to the crowd.

wordDefs.def: A fight by many people against the people in power
ex: The uprising began in the capital and spread fast.
Her father fought in the uprising as a young man.
A statue in the square honors the uprising.

wordDefs.def: Normal people who are not rich, famous or powerful
ex: High prices hurt ordinary people the most.
The show tells the stories of ordinary people.
Ordinary people raised money for the new hospital.

wordDefs.def: People who work at the same place as you
ex: I eat lunch with my coworkers on Fridays.
Her coworkers gave her a card for her birthday.
He likes all of his coworkers.

wordDefs.def: Forced to do something by a threat to tell your secrets
ex: The manager was blackmailed over an old mistake.
She was blackmailed with private photos.
He paid money because he was being blackmailed.

wordDefs.def: Statements that someone will hurt you if you do not obey
ex: The company received threats by email.
He reported the threats to the police.
She kept working in spite of the threats.

wordDefs.def: Guessed carefully from the facts you have
ex: An estimated 500 people came to the concert.
The repairs have an estimated cost of 2,000 dollars.
An estimated ten percent of the town has no internet.
The new bridge is far from complete.
Our list of guests is far from complete.
The report is far from complete and needs more work.

wordDefs.def: Cut into very thin pieces so no one can read it
ex: The office shredded all its old bills.
My bank statements get shredded after a year.
He shredded the letter and threw it in the trash.

wordDefs.def: A win in an election by a very large number of votes
ex: The governor won a landslide victory last time.
No one expected such a landslide victory.
A landslide victory gave the party full control.

wordDefs.def: Something a candidate says they will do if elected
ex: Lower taxes were his main campaign promise.
The mayor kept her campaign promise on buses.
Voters remember every broken campaign promise.

wordDefs.def: People who study and write about the past
ex: Historians still study that war.
Historians found the old letters in a church.
Many historians visit this library.

wordDefs.def: People who say what is wrong with a plan or idea
ex: Critics say the new law is unfair.
Critics of the plan want a new vote.
The mayor answered her critics at the meeting.

wordDefs.def: Strong disagreement between groups of people
ex: The new law caused division in our town.
Money can cause division in a family.
The vote showed a deep division in the country.

wordDefs.def: The respect that every person deserves
ex: Nurses treat every patient with dignity.
Older people want to live with dignity.
She handled the bad news with dignity.

mainIdea.s: Hungary has placed about 60,000 names from communist-era secret police records on a public website. The move may help people face the past, but a name alone does not prove anyone was an informer.
mainIdea.why: Anyone can now look up the names. Historians warn that some people turned down requests to become informers and still ended up in the records.

mainIdea.s: Hungarians can now read every report that informers wrote during those decades. Historians believe these complete files finally show exactly who worked for the government and who refused to help it.
mainIdea.why: Close, but the website leaves out the reports informers wrote, and many files were shredded. A name on the website does not prove someone was an informer.

mainIdea.s: Courts in Budapest will soon try several former officers for crimes committed during the 1956 revolution. Relatives of the victims plan to attend, and the trials could last for more than two years.
mainIdea.why: There are no trials here. Hungary put names from old secret police records online, and some families may find out hard facts about relatives.

tf.s: Anyone can now look up names from Hungary's secret police records online.
tf.why: About 60,000 names went on a public website on the anniversary of the Soviet attack on Budapest in 1956.

tf.s: A name on the website proves that the person worked as an informer.
tf.why: Historians warn that it does not. Some people turned down requests to become informers and still ended up in the records.

tf.s: Hungarian governments quickly opened the files after communist rule ended.
tf.why: Both left and right governments put off opening the files for decades after 1989.

tf.s: Some families may find out that a deceased relative was an informer.
tf.why: The prime minister said many families will face difficult information, and he asked for dignity and humanity.

tf.s: The website includes the reports that informers wrote about other people.
tf.why: The website leaves out those reports, to protect the people the informers watched.

tf.s: Critics say the website comes too late and may cause pain.
tf.why: They also fear division. The government says the website will help Hungarians get over the past.

lines.text: Did you hear that Hungary put its old secret police records online?
Secret police? From the communist years?
Yes. Anyone can {{look up}} a name now. There are about 60,000 names on the website.
So you could {{find out}} your grandfather was an informer? That's a lot of [[skeletons in the closet]].
Right. And many of those people were blackmailed before they {{passed on}} information about friends and neighbors.
That's hard to judge. I've never been [[in their shoes]].
Critics worry about that too. They think people will judge too quickly.
Why did this take so long? Communist rule ended in 1989.
One government after another {{put off}} opening the files.
Maybe nobody wanted to [[open a can of worms]].
Maybe. Also, a lot of files are gone. Many were shredded when communist rule {{fell apart}}.
So does a name on the website prove anything?
Not always. Some people {{turned down}} requests to become informers and still {{ended up}} in the records.
No. And the website {{leaves out}} the reports informers wrote. Longer files {{come out}} by late February.
Part of me says [[let sleeping dogs lie]].
Prime Minister Peter Magyar disagrees. He says people can't {{get over}} a painful past without talking about it.
I just hope people treat those families with some dignity.

expressions.def: Used to talk about embarrassing or shameful secrets from someone's past
ex: Every family has a few skeletons in the closet.
The senator says he has no skeletons in the closet.

expressions.def: Used to imagine being in the difficult situation of other people
ex: It's easy to criticize when you've never been in their shoes.

expressions.def: To start something that will cause many new problems
ex: Asking about the will could open a can of worms.

expressions.def: Used to say a situation is complicated, with no simple right or wrong
ex: The answer is not black and white.
Family money problems are not black and white.

expressions.def: Used to say that old problems are better left alone
ex: I wanted to ask about their fight, but I decided to let sleeping dogs lie.
